procedural_history.originating_court: Deputy Commissioner of Police, Traffic Branch, Ahmedabad City
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of externment passed under s. 56 of the Act, challenged via notice dated August 13, 1964, served under s. 59 read with s. 56 of the Act.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent in Criminal Appeal 167/65 filed Special Criminal Application No. 3 of 1965 in the Gujarat High Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, seeking to quash the order of externment. The High Court struck down the orders of externment as containing vague allegations. Special Criminal Application No. 8 of 1965 was also directed against the order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Deputy Commissioner of Police, Traffic Branch, Ahmedabad City appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgments and orders dated April 8, 1965, of the Gujarat High Court in Special Criminal Applications Nos. 3 and 8 of 1965. The Supreme Court held that the High Court was in error.

directions: The orders of the Gujarat High Court are set aside.
No action can be taken against the respondents in these appeals on the basis of the orders which are now held to be valid.

issue.issue_text: Whether the writ petitions filed by the respondents in the High Court should have been entertained when they had not exhausted their alternative remedy of appeal under Section 60 of the Act.

facts: The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution to challenge externment orders made against them.
The respondents had an alternative remedy available to them: an appeal to the State Government under Section 60 of the Act.
The appellant argued that the High Court should not have entertained the writ petitions because the respondents had failed to exhaust this alternative remedy.
law: The High Court has jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution to entertain writ petitions.
The existence of an alternative remedy does not automatically bar the High Court's jurisdiction; the court has the discretion to entertain a petition despite an unexhausted remedy.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court, in exercising its jurisdiction, had made a conscious decision not to reject the respondents' petitions on the ground that they had not exhausted their remedy of appeal.
The Supreme Court deferred to the High Court's exercise of its discretion in this matter.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no merit in the appellant's argument. It held that since the High Court had chosen to exercise its jurisdiction and entertain the petitions, despite the available alternative remedy, the Supreme Court would not interfere with that decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court correctly interpreted Section 59 of the Act and was justified in striking down the orders of externment.

facts: The respondents were issued externment orders under Section 56 of an Act, based on notices issued under Section 59.
The respondents challenged these orders in the High Court, arguing that the notices under Section 59 were invalid.

The respondents claimed the allegations in the notices were "too vague and general, both with regard to the time and places of his alleged activities," which prevented them from offering an effective explanation or defense.
The High Court agreed with the respondents, finding the notices invalid due to vagueness, and consequently struck down the externment orders.
law: Section 59 of the Act requires that before an externment order is passed, the person must be informed of the general nature of the material allegations against them and be given a reasonable opportunity to offer an explanation.
The Supreme Court noted that it had previously rendered decisions upholding the validity of Sections 56 and 59 of the Act, which the High Court had not referenced.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's conclusion that the notices were too vague.
The Court found that the notices were "strictly in accordance with s. 59, of the Act."
It determined that the respondents had been given a reasonable opportunity to tender an explanation regarding the allegations made against them.
The Court pointed out that similar arguments regarding the vagueness of notices under Section 59 had already been dealt with and rejected in its own prior decisions.
Therefore, the Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's justification for striking down the orders—that the allegations were vague—was incorrect.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had incorrectly interpreted Section 59 of the Act. It held that the notices were not invalid for vagueness and that the respondents had been given a reasonable opportunity to defend themselves. Consequently, the Supreme Court found that the High Court was not justified in striking down the externment orders, and it set aside the High Court's judgment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the writ petitions filed by the respondents in the High Court should have been entertained when they had not exhausted their alternative remedy of appeal under Section 60 of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The writ petitions filed by the respondents in the High Court should not have been entertained because they had an alternative remedy of appeal to the State Government under Section 60 of the Act, which they had not exhausted.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondents' counter-argument, but their action of filing the writ petitions implies they believed the High Court's intervention was warranted despite the alternative remedy.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court correctly interpreted Section 59 of the Act and was justified in striking down the orders of externment.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in striking down the orders of externment for containing vague allegations, as the notices issued were strictly in accordance with Section 59 of the Act.
respondent_arguments: The views expressed by the High Court were correct, and the notices under Section 59 and the subsequent orders of externment were invalid and rightly quashed.

cases.principle: The Act is based on the principle that it is desirable in the larger interests of society that the freedom of movement and residence of a few people should be restrained so the majority of the community may live in peace, and that an individual's right to reside and move freely must yield to the larger interests of the community.
It was cited for its consideration of the specific scope of s. 56 of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An externment order based on a notice that is in accordance with section 59 of the Act cannot be struck down on the grounds of containing vague allegations. Furthermore, a High Court's decision to exercise its writ jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227, despite the existence of an alternative statutory remedy, is a matter of its discretion and will not be interfered with on appeal merely because the alternative remedy was not exhausted.
obiter: The Act is based on the principle that it is desirable in the larger interests of society that the freedom of movement and residence of a comparatively fewer number of people should be restrained, so that the majority of the community may live in peace and harmony.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was in error for striking down the orders of externment. The High Court failed to consider and apply binding precedents from this Court which had already held the relevant sections of the Act (Sections 56 and 59) to be valid. The notices issued under Section 59 were in accordance with the law, and the High Court was not justified in finding them to be vague.
legal_tests_applied: The doctrine of precedent, requiring lower courts to follow the binding decisions of higher courts, specifically the Supreme Court's prior rulings on the validity of Sections 56 and 59 of the Act.
why_appellant_lost: On the issue of alternative remedy, the appellant's argument was rejected because the Supreme Court saw no merit in interfering with the High Court's discretionary choice to exercise its jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227, even though the respondents had not exhausted their statutory appeal.

Regarding the first contention, we see no merit, especially when the High Court, in the exercise of its jurisdiction, under Arts. 226 and 227, has not chosen to reject the· applications, filed by the respondents, on the ground that they had not exhausted their remedy of appeal, under s. 60, of the Act.
why_respondent_won: On the issue of alternative remedy, the respondent's position was upheld because the Supreme Court deferred to the High Court's discretion in deciding to hear the writ petitions.

Regarding the first contention, we see no merit, especially when the High Court, in the exercise of its jurisdiction, under Arts. 226 and 227, has not chosen to reject the· applications, filed by the respondents, on the ground that they had not exhausted their remedy of appeal, under s. 60, of the Act.
policy_considerations: The Act is based on the principle that it is desirable, in the larger interests of society, that the freedom of movement, and residence of a comparatively fewer number of people, should be restrained, so that the majority of the community may move and live in peace and harmony, and carry on their peaceful avocations untrammelled by any fear or threat of violence to their person or property.
The individual's right to reside in and move freely in any part of the territory of India, has to yield to the larger interests of the community.
